newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE-HK to drive China, says "Red capitalist".
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK to drive China, says "Red capitalist".

text.p: "Red capitalist" Shen Zuyu, one of the richest men in the old Shanghai, lost almost everything after the communists came in 1949 because he decided to stay rather than go with many of his friends to Hong Kong.

Now, capitalist Hong Kong is returning to the communists, at midnight on June 30. But this time, it is the capitalists who will more likely set the pace, pushing China towards faster and deeper reforms, Shen believes.
"The return of Hong Kong will have a good effect in promoting the development of China," said Shen, 77.

"There are many good things about Hong Kong, particularly the way in which companies there are run. The whole theoretical basis of the system in China is more backward," he said in an interview. "Hong Kong is going to push China forward."

Shen, once the owner of a huge wood oil exporting firm, considered moving to Hong Kong in 1948 as the communists approached Shanghai. But in the end he decided to stay, thereby earning the title "red capitalist".
NO TURNING BACK

It was one of those fateful decisions from which there was no turning back. By the late 1950s, his company and most of his assets had been seized, but Shen says he doesn't regret his decision not to go to Hong Kong, which was based partly on family obligations and partly on a negative reaction to the place.

"I went to Hong Kong to have a look in 1948 but it was too small," he said. Many of Shen's assets were returned and he is living comfortably on the income, despite a difficult period earlier which he is reluctant to speak of.
"I cannot complain. At least I survived, I'm still here," he said with a laugh.
Shanghai industrialists who did go to Hong Kong used their capital, their machinery and their experience to help turn Hong Kong into a modern economic powerhouse, while Shanghai languished.
But even if he had gone to Hong Kong, Shen said there was no guarantee that he would have remained wealthy and at the forefront of commerce.
"Rich people are conservative, they don't adapt easily to changes. The rich people in Hong Kong now were not so rich then," he said.
WE WANT TO BE MODERN
Shen said capitalism was a more efficient system, but added that stark comparisons between socialism and capitalism were no longer so relevant.
"Forget the "isms", what we want to be is modern," he said.

"The capitalism of today is not the capitalism of the past. The capitalism of today includes social services, which have nothing to do with what Marx talked about. And private firms have become stock companies with ordinary people holding shares," he said.
China's small private enterprise sector will grow, but will always remain a minor part of the overall economy, Shen said.
He believes the focus of its development should be on opening up the huge state-owned enterprises to private investors.
"The state enterprises need to become stock-holding companies. This is not a matter of privatisation or capitalism, it's a matter of becoming more modern," he said.
POLITICAL REFORM LIKELY
Shen also predicted reform and change in China's political sphere, though more slowly than in the economic arena.
"There'll be gradual development on the political front. We need greater regulation, a stronger rule of law, less of Communist Party leaders having the last say on issues," Shen said.

Asked how corruption in China today compared with the old Nationalist government before 1949, Shen said: "You can't compare it directly. In the old days, administration and business were separated, now they are the same person, so it's very difficult to tell."

"For example, you have the Public Security Bureau running nightclubs, and the Commercial Administration Bureau running companies. People react against this kind of thing strongly. It's been getting worse and worse in recent years," he said.
